prompt:
Which statements about the median-of-medians algorithm are true? Select all that apply.

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.text: With groups of 5, the pivot has roughly three tenths of the input size elements on each side
options.explanation: Correct. Half the group medians are ≤ the pivot, and each brings two more smaller elements from its group: about three tenths of the input size.

options.text: The two recursive size fractions are one fifth and at most seven tenths, with linear partition work
options.explanation: Correct. One recursive call finds the median of the one fifth of the input size medians; the other continues on at most about seven tenths of the input size elements.

options.text: With groups of 3 instead, the same analysis gives only O(n log n)
options.explanation: Correct. For the simple groups-of-three analysis, the two recursive size fractions sum to one. This gives only a logarithmic-factor linear upper bound, rather than a linear guarantee.

options.text: It is usually faster than randomised quickselect in practice
options.explanation: No. The extra grouping and pivot selection often adds overhead; exact speed depends on implementation. Some hybrids use it as a fallback.

options.text: Introselect uses it (or a similar guaranteed method) as a fallback when quickselect makes poor progress
options.explanation: Correct. A linear fallback with a suitable progress budget can give worst-case linear work. Heap-fallback introselect need not; ordinary C++ nth_element requires only average linear complexity.

workedExample:
The key test for this kind of recursion: do the two recursive calls **together** receive less than the whole input? If they do, each level does a fixed fraction less work than the one above, and those shrinking amounts add up to a linear total. If they receive the whole input, every level costs about as much as the first and the levels add up to n log n.

| Group size | Combined recursive fraction | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | Full input across both calls | O(n log n) |
| 5 | Nine tenths in both calls | O(n) |
| 7 | Six sevenths in both calls | O(n) |

The guarantee costs extra work per element, which is why randomised quickselect is the default and median of medians the safety net.

prompt: An attacker who knows your code submits 1,000 distinct numbers to a median-of-medians selector (groups of 5). What can you say about the size of the recursive call after the first partition?

options.text: At most 500, because the median of medians is the true median
options.explanation: The median of the group medians is only near the middle, not exactly at it. The guarantee is weaker than a perfect split, but it holds for every input.

options.text: At most about 700 (roughly seven tenths), whatever order the attacker chooses
options.explanation: Correct. At least three elements from each of about half the groups lie on each side of the pivot, so roughly three tenths of the input is always discarded. The conservative finite bound excludes at least 294 elements, leaving at most 706.

options.text: At most about 800, because only the group medians are known to be on the right side
options.explanation: That counts only the medians themselves (a fifth of the input). Each median below the pivot also brings the two smaller members of its group, which triples the guaranteed fraction.

options.text: Up to 999, because a crafted input can still push the pivot to one end
options.explanation: That is the risk with plain quickselect and a predictable pivot. Median of medians computes its pivot from the data in a way that always leaves a fixed fraction on each side, so no input can force a one-element shrink.

workedExample:
1. 1,000 elements form 200 groups of five, so there are 200 group medians.
2. The pivot M is the median of those 200 medians, so about 100 of them are no larger than M.
3. Each of those medians has two smaller members in its own group, so about 3 × 100 = 300 elements are guaranteed to be no larger than M. By symmetry about 300 are no smaller.
4. Allowing for M's own group and the ragged last group, the textbook bound guarantees at least 294 on each side, so the side you recurse into has at most 706 elements.

This holds for every input, including adversarial ones: each round discards at least about 29% of the elements, guaranteed.
